item.title: agent_learning: An Open-Source AI Agent Development Textbook
item.description:
agent_learning: An Open-Source AI Agent Development Textbook

An open-source AI Agent textbook and learning repository called agent_learning has been released to address the skill gap between calling an LLM API and building a complete Agent system. The resource provides a systematic tutorial covering the full lifecycle of agent development, from foundational concepts to production deployment.

🧩 How it works

The textbook is structured to guide developers through the core components of agentic systems. It covers the transition from basic capabilities to advanced deployment strategies, including:

  • Core Capabilities: Function calling, memory systems, planning, RAG, and context engineering.
  • Advanced Topics: Agentic RL, multi-agent systems, and self-evolving agents.
  • Production Readiness: Evaluation, security, and deployment pipelines.

The curriculum includes 26 chapters organized across six main areas: foundations, core capabilities, frameworks, multi-agent systems, production, and capstone projects. The material bridges theoretical papers and practical application by providing explanations for techniques such as ReAct, Reflexion, MemGPT/Letta, GraphRAG, and GRPO.

⚙️ Key details

The repository is designed for bilingual accessibility and includes substantial visual aids to support complex concepts.

Feature Description
Language Support English and Chinese editions with matching tables of contents
Visual Resources 330+ original SVG diagrams and 5 interactive demos
Practical Baseline reference-agent/ folder with a runnable baseline including tools, memory, and security gates
Code Structure Separate sources for English (src/en/) and Chinese (src/zh/) mdBooks

The chapter structure includes specific deep dives into:

  • Frameworks: LangChain, LangGraph, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Claude Code, and OpenCode V2.
  • Techniques: Harness Engineering, Skills, and Context Engineering.
  • Advanced Systems: Multimodal Agents and DeepSeek Harness.

💡 Why it matters

The agent_learning repository is explicitly designed for developers who have moved past simple API integration and need to build, evaluate, secure, and deploy Agent systems. By combining theoretical paper-to-practice explanations with runnable code baselines and interactive demos, it serves as a comprehensive reference for both individual developers and teams looking to standardize their AI agent development workflows.

item.title: Autumn-27 ARTEX Open-Source Fork Now Maintained by ChainReactors
item.description:
Autumn-27 ARTEX Open-Source Fork Now Maintained by ChainReactors

The Autumn-27/ARTEX project, an AI autonomous penetration testing system originally built with a Go backend and Next.js frontend, has seen its open-source continuation. The repository RuoJi6/ARTEX is a fork of the original Autumn-27/ARTEX, preserving the upstream commit history and AGPL-3.0 license. It is now maintained by ChainReactors.

🧩 How it works

The system integrates with external data sources to streamline asset collection. Specifically, it supports direct synchronization of asset data from ScopeSentry, eliminating the need for manual repeated collection. Users configure the ScopeSentry address and API key on the “Asset Sync” page, select targets and asset types (such as domains, subdomains, IPs, ports, sites, or endpoints) by project or task dimension, and import data to merge it into the ARTEX asset graph for agent exploration.

⚙️ Key details

  • Database & LLM: The system depends on PostgreSQL and requires an LLM configuration for exploration, supporting either ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY (configurable via CLI or UI).
  • MCP Support: Remote MCP can be configured in system settings using http (Streamable HTTP) or sse (legacy SSE).
  • Dockerization: The ruoji6/artex Docker image is built and published via GitHub Actions. It includes common tools like ripgrep, curl, vim, npm, and nmap. The image supports linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 architectures, with Docker automatically selecting the matching host architecture.
  • Persistence: The ./skills and ./data directories are persisted via bind mounts.

🚀 Availability

  • Docker Setup: The installation script automatically detects and installs Docker. Users can choose between “All Docker” (which generates a .env file and runs docker compose up -d) or local compilation.
  • Local Setup: For local runs, users select a database option, generate a config.json, and compile an embedded single binary.
  • Access: After installation, the service is accessible at http://localhost:8787, requiring an initial setup at /setup to set the admin password.
  • Download: Release packages are available for download from the repository’s Releases page. Linux ARM64 users (including ARM64 Kali) should select the linux-arm64 build, while x86_64 users select linux-amd64.
  • Execution: Users must launch the application using start.sh or start.bat rather than running ./artex directly. These scripts act as daemons that restart the program based on exit codes, which is required for the “one-click update” feature to function correctly.

item.title: LightlySSL Adds World Model Training with LeWM for Image-based Agents
item.description:
LightlySSL Adds World Model Training with LeWM for Image-based Agents

LightlySSL, a Python library and computer vision framework for self-supervised learning and latent world models on images, has introduced new world model training capabilities. The update allows the system to learn how a scene responds to actions using the LeWM architecture, enabling planning in its own embedding space.

🧩 How it works

The new LeWM component learns from raw frames and actions without requiring rewards, labels, or a map of the environment. It trains through random play. Once trained, the model plans by imagining the outcome of each move within its embedding space. This allows agents to find paths to goals, such as navigating through a door to a target location, based solely on a picture of that goal.

⚙️ Key details

LightlySSL is built with a modular framework that exposes low-level building blocks, including loss functions and model heads. It is written in a PyTorch-like style and supports custom backbone models for self-supervised pre-training. The framework also supports distributed training using PyTorch Lightning.

Users can access the functionality by installing the library with PyTorch version 2.0 or later.

Component Description
LeWM Learns scene responses to actions from raw frames and plans via imagined outcomes
LeJEPA Self-supervised learning support added in May 2026
LightlyStudio Open-source project for visualizing, annotating, and managing data
LightlyTrain New project making SSL and distillation pretraining accessible in a few lines of code

🚀 Availability

The library is available for installation via pip. A commercial version is offered with additional features, including Docker support and pretraining models for embedding, classification, detection, and segmentation tasks. This commercial version also includes a platform with active learning and data curation features.

item.title: Idun Agent Platform Is No Longer Maintained as Open-Source Project
item.description:
Idun Agent Platform Is No Longer Maintained as Open-Source Project

The Idun Agent Platform is no longer maintained. Its code stays open source under the GPLv3 license, and its official documentation remains online for reference.

🔍 Overview

Idun Agent Platform was created as an open-source, self-hosted production wrapper for LangGraph and Google ADK agents. It allows developers to deploy agents as production-ready FastAPI services without vendor lock-in.

Teams building AI agents typically face a tradeoff: building a custom production wrapper (combining FastAPI, traces, guardrails, and an admin UI), which is slow, or adopting SaaS solutions like LangGraph Cloud or LangSmith, which introduces sovereignty trade-offs. Idun provided a third path by offering a self-sufficient FastAPI process installed via a single pip install command on local or private infrastructure.

⚙️ Key details

The platform is distributed as a single wheel bundling three Python packages:

Package Description
idun_agent_engine The engine SDK providing the FastAPI app factory, Model Context Protocol (MCP) registry, observability, and guardrails.
idun_agent_standalone Provides the idun CLI, admin REST API, and UIs for chat, administration, and traces.
idun_agent_schema Contains the Pydantic configuration schemas.

Built-in platform capabilities and features include:

  • AG-UI copilotkit API and bundled chat UI
  • Admin panel and managed prompts
  • 15+ guardrails
  • MCP tool governance
  • OpenTelemetry observability and dedicated trace store
  • OIDC and SSO integration
  • Memory persistence and messaging integrations

🛠️ Usage details

  • Prerequisites: Python 3.12 or 3.13.
  • Installation: pip install idun-agent-engine.
  • CLI: The idun executable provides commands including setup, serve, init, hash-password, and agent serve via idun_agent_standalone.
  • Workflow: Users create a directory (such as my-agent/), save the required files, and run the engine from within that directory or via an absolute path.
  • Path Resolution: The graph_definition: "./agent.py:graph" setting is resolved relative to the directory where idun init is run.
  • Endpoints: Launching the service opens a chat UI at http://localhost:8000. Settings, MCP servers, guardrails, and SSO are configured at /admin, while trace data is available at /admin/traces.

🚀 Availability

  • Maintenance Status: No longer maintained.
  • Licensing: Code remains available open source under GPLv3.
  • Documentation: Stays online for developer reference.

MCPM v2.0 releases a global configuration model for MCP servers

MCPM v2.0 has been released as an open source CLI tool for managing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. This version eliminates the complexity of the v1 target-based system in favor of a clean global workspace model, allowing users to install servers once and organize them with profiles before integrating them into various MCP clients.

🔍 Overview

MCPM provides a simplified approach to managing MCP servers through a global configuration model. Instead of managing individual targets, users can now install servers once and use them everywhere. The tool is designed to be AI Agent Friendly, offering a non-interactive CLI with comprehensive automation support and an llm.txt guide.

🧩 How it works

The v2.0 architecture uses a global configuration model where servers are installed once and organized with virtual profiles. These profiles act as tags to organize servers into logical groups for different workflows. Once organized, servers can be integrated into specific MCP clients as needed.

item.title: Music gear companies open-source devices in response to AI vibe-coding
item.description:
Music gear companies open-source devices in response to AI vibe-coding

The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools has created chaos in the music gear world, forcing companies to determine how to respond to a wave of AI-aided custom firmwares and modding communities. While some manufacturers have remained silent, others have decided to embrace the trend by opening up their devices and providing tools for the community.

🔍 Overview

As it became clear that no piece of music gear was safe from AI tools and curious tinkerers, companies began making their devices open source. Major names like inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, and Native Instruments, decided to “join ’em” rather than resist. Meanwhile, companies like Roland, Korg, Arturia, and Novation have yet to issue public statements on the matter.

⚙️ Key details

  • inMusic: inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell stated the company will provide a toolbox and the inner workings of devices like the MPC or Sample so people can do what they want. This includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key. Akai aims to walk a fine line by offering modders access while keeping products reliable for professionals, promising a “reset button” so users can experiment without losing their original setup.
  • Behringer: The company announced a slew of open-source devices, including a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller. Launch dates for these products are currently unclear.
  • M-Vave: The company’s $70 pocketable clone of the Yamaha DX7 became popular due to its price and hackability, leading to more than a dozen custom firmwares. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware for developers and confirmed its successor, the FM-2, will also be open source.
  • Erica Synths: The company released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine. Founder Ģirts Ozoliņš noted the sustainability of using one device with various options instead of buying multiple “plastic boxes,” while acknowledging that vibe coding does not offset the environmental impact of data centers.
  • Polyend: Open-sourced its line of Tracker grooveboxes and released the Endless guitar pedal last year, which allows users to vibe-code their own effects.
  • Elektron: The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, warning that modifications could brick machines, prevent updates, or affect warranty coverage. CPO Christian Alsing stated that while he is sympathetic to the hacker community and believes users have the right to modify their devices, he pushed back on accusations that the company is withholding features.

💡 Why it matters

The shift toward open-sourcing hardware and firmware reflects a strategic pivot in the music technology industry. Companies are balancing the potential for community innovation and sustainability against the risks of hardware instability and the environmental costs associated with AI development.

item.title: OpenQodex adds pre-push code review for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor
item.description:
OpenQodex adds pre-push code review for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor

Open source code review tool OpenQodex now runs inside coding agents to check every change before you push. It operates without requiring a separate account or API key, acting as a separate reviewer that validates code changes made by agents in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Cline.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenQodex is an open source code review tool for coding agents.
  • It runs a separate reviewer that checks every change an agent writes before the user pushes.
  • No account or key of its own is required.
  • It is available for use in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Cline.

🧩 How it works

  • Code Graph: A code graph provides the agent with a map of the codebase.
  • Scanner Integration: It runs scanners that fit the changed files, keeping findings on the changed lines. A scanner is a program that checks code without a model, such as gitleaks or semgrep.
  • Dependency Check: Every supported lockfile in the repository is checked against osv.dev at every review and scan of a change. Advisories outside the changed lines are shown but never counted.
  • Fresh Reviewers: Separate Claude Code or Codex processes on the user’s login run the review, with no memory of the current session.
  • Verification: A script checks every line a reviewer quotes as evidence against the code. Verifiers confirm or refute every candidate and every scanner finding.

⚙️ Key details

  • Initiation: Users say to their agent, “review my change with openqodex”.
  • Setup: The init command finds agents on the machine, lists the files it will write, and asks for confirmation once.
  • Terminal Execution: In your own terminal, run ~/.openqodex/bin/openqodex review.
  • Sandbox Limitation: In its default sandbox, Codex gives commands no network, so the terminal command must be run outside the sandbox.
  • Scope: The review covers commits not yet pushed plus everything uncommitted.
  • Output: The tool prints a receipt with the verdict, one line per finding, and the path to report.html. It also writes report.md, report.json, and report.sarif.

🚀 Availability

  • Works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Cline, and Goose.
  • The host identifier can be claude-code, codex, cursor, cline, or goose.
  • An npx install does not put OpenQodex on the system PATH.
  • The reviewer was tested with Claude Code 2.1.330 using claude-opus-5-5.

item.title: OpenAI and Cisco Launch Open-Source Shirudo Security Tool
item.description:
OpenAI and Cisco Launch Open-Source Shirudo Security Tool

OpenAI and Cisco launched an open-source Linux security tool named Shirudo. The tool deploys temporary runtime protections to block vulnerability exploitation while administrators prepare and roll out patches, allowing operators to do so without restarting services.

🧩 How it works

Shirudo leverages the eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) mechanism in Linux to monitor for suspicious activity and deploy targeted protections called “shields.” eBPF is a Linux technology that lets programs run in a controlled environment within the operating system’s kernel without modifying its source code or requiring a restart.

The tool’s capabilities include:

  • Live protection: Blocks vulnerable code paths without restarting systems, letting operators assess shield impact before enforcing them.
  • AI-assisted defense: Enables agents to investigate vulnerabilities, develop shields, and validate their effectiveness, with deployment remaining under human control.
  • Trusted deployment: Uses cryptographic signatures, Linux’s eBPF verifier, and kernel security controls to prevent unauthorized modifications.
  • Hardware-backed verification: Uses Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) to provide verifiable records of shields being loaded or removed.

Shirudo is designed for an agentic control plane with a configurable degree of autonomy when deploying mitigations. When a shield is deployed, the tool provides operators with hit counts, giving them insight into attempted exploits and where defenses need strengthening. Isovalent states that Shirudo is not limited to eBPF and can also modify application or userspace runtime bytecode to extend protection where needed.

⚙️ Key details

Shirudo is a rewrite of Tetragon, an open-source eBPF-based runtime security platform introduced by Isovalent in 2022. Tetragon also serves as the foundation for Cisco’s existing Live Protect technology. Isovalent, a cloud networking and security company acquired by Cisco in 2024, developed the tool.

Component Description
Test Case Researchers demonstrated that custom-generated shields could successfully block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without interrupting its operation.
Distribution Shields will be distributed as cryptographically signed ‘.bee’ packages through an OCI registry.
Execution The tool can be activated through a command-line interface and doesn’t require a daemon to run permanently on the machine.
Compatibility The tool’s capabilities are limited to Linux because Mac and Windows have not implemented the components needed to be effective, according to Marcus Hutchins of Expel.

The two companies plan to provide “ready-to-use” mitigations in the form of tested shields, along with vulnerability disclosures, until patching is possible. While there is “genuinely so much runtime exploit mitigation potential with eBPF,” Marcus Hutchins noted that it may not be a good idea to let AI agents write rules that could impact the kernel.

🚀 Availability

Shirudo is open-source under BSD and GPL licenses. It comes with a quick-start guide as well as “getting started” documentation from Isovalent. On December 15, OpenAI will provide a technical rundown of how the tool works and how it combines eBPF and artificial intelligence to detect and counter new attacks in a deep-dive webinar.

item.description:
Google and Partners Introduce A2A Protocol for AI Agent Communication

A2A (Agent2Agent) is an open protocol from Google and partners enabling different AI agents from various vendors and frameworks to communicate securely and collaborate on tasks. The protocol aims to break down silos between isolated agent systems, allowing for more complex cross-application automation.

⚙️ Key details

  • Simple: Uses existing standards including HTTP, JSON-RPC, and SSE.
  • Enterprise Ready: Focuses on Auth, Security, Privacy, and Monitoring.
  • Async First: Handles long-running tasks and human-in-the-loop scenarios.
  • Modality Agnostic: Supports Text, Files, Forms, and Streams.
  • Opaque Execution: Agents interact without sharing internal logic or tools.
  • Discovery: Agents publish an Agent Card in JSON describing capabilities, endpoints, and authentication needs.
  • Communication: A Client agent sends a Task request containing a Message with Parts to a Remote Agent Server using HTTP/JSON-RPC 2.0.
  • Execution & Response: The Server processes the task, updates its status, and responds with the final status and generated Artifacts containing Parts.
  • Streaming: For long tasks, the Server can optionally stream TaskStatusUpdateEvent or TaskArtifactUpdateEvent via Server-Sent Events (SSE) or use Push Notifications.

item.title: OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography
item.description:
OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography

OpenNHP is a lightweight, cryptography-powered, open-source toolkit implementing Zero Trust security for infrastructure, applications, and data. It serves as the reference implementation of the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP) specification.

🔍 Overview

OpenNHP is designed to hide servers, ports, and domains from the public internet. In the AI era, visibility equates to vulnerability; OpenNHP inverts this model by remaining invisible until trusted. Consequently, scanners, bots, and AI-driven attackers find nothing to attack because nothing answers until a client proves its identity with a single encrypted packet.

🧩 How it works

The toolkit features two core protocols and a modular design inspired by the NIST Zero Trust Architecture:

  • Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP): Conceals server ports, IP addresses, and domain names to protect applications and infrastructure from unauthorized access.
  • Data-content Hiding Protocol (DHP): Ensures data security and privacy via encryption and confidential computing, making data “usable but not visible.”

The architecture includes specific components that slot alongside existing IAM, DNS, FIDO, and Zero Trust policy engines:

Component Function
NHP-Agent Client that sends encrypted knock requests to gain access
NHP-Server Authenticates and authorizes requests; runs separately and is architecturally decoupled from the protected host
NHP-AC Access controller that manages firewall rules on the protected server
NHP-Relay HTTP-to-UDP bridge enabling browser-based agents to send NHP knocks via HTTPS
NHP-KGC Key Generation Center for Identity-Based Cryptography (IBC)

The workflow operates on a default-deny gate for every port, IP, and hostname:

  1. Registration (once per device): The agent generates its own key pair and enrolls the public key. The agent requests a one-time password (NHP_OTP), which the Server’s auth plugin delivers to the user (e.g., by email). The agent sends the OTP and its public key (NHP_REG), and the Server binds the key to the user and replies (NHP_RAK). The private key never leaves the device.
  2. Knock (every access): The agent sends an encrypted knock (NHP_KNK) to the Server. The Server validates the knock and sends an operation.

💡 Why it matters

Attackers can’t exploit what they can’t discover. NHP represents a next step in “hide the service first” designs, extending security stacks rather than forking them.

item.title: Critical PHP and Drupal Security Updates Released
item.description:
Critical PHP and Drupal Security Updates Released

On November 19, security updates were released for 18 vulnerabilities in the PHP development ecosystem, alongside the patching of a critical remote code execution flaw in the Drupal content management system. These updates address severe security issues that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable servers.

🚀 PHP Security Updates

The PHP dev team released updates for all supported branches, with versions 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 now available. Security firm Aikido reports that these updates address 18 CVEs affecting PHP’s core engine, session handling, PHP-FPM, CGI, and other components. The most serious flaw, CVE-2026-129289, is a critical PHP-FPM request smuggling vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.2. This vulnerability affects certain nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM; standard configurations that do not reuse connections are not affected. As a temporary mitigation, administrators can disable persistent backend connections to ensure they are closed after each request. Third-party maintainer Ondrej Surý has released patched packages for unsupported versions back to PHP 5.6, and Aikido has released hardened container images for similar unsupported versions.

🧩 PHP Vulnerability Details

The following vulnerabilities were fixed in the November updates:

CVE Identifier Description
CVE-2026-129474 Use-after-free vulnerability involving magic method backtraces
CVE-2026-129496 Timezone cache use-after-free vulnerability
CVE-2026-126714 Vulnerability involving partially overwritten session files
CVE-2026-115560 Session serializer mismatch vulnerability
CVE-2026-129291 PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free vulnerability
CVE-2026-128090 PHAR OpenSSL signature bypass vulnerability

Additional fixes address memory corruption, information disclosure, cross-site scripting, denial-of-service issues, and unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs. As a temporary mitigation for CVE-2026-115560, PHP recommended disabling session upload progress by setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0. This vulnerability was disclosed in an October 23 informational advisory.

🛡️ Drupal Critical Flaws

The Drupal Security Team has patched a critical remote code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165. Discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, this flaw allows anonymous users to exploit the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, potentially leading to site takeover or remote code execution. The security team warned that at least one critical vulnerability can be exploited by anonymous users. Drupal administrators are urged to upgrade to versions 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13. For those who cannot immediately upgrade, it is recommended to secure the Drupal installer by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file. This update also addresses a moderately critical gadget chain vulnerability (CVE-2026-132166). The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged five Drupal vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021.

  • qdrant-find: Retrieves relevant information from the Qdrant database.

Configuration Details

Configuration is handled via environment variables, and the only command-line argument is --transport, which selects the transport protocol. You cannot provide both QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_LOCAL_PATH simultaneously.

Environment Variable Description
QDRANT_LOCAL_PATH Path to the local Qdrant database (alternative to QDRANT_URL)

FASTMCP_PORT Port to run the server on (SSE and HTTP transports)
FASTMCP_MASK_ERROR_DETAILS Hide exception details from tool error messages sent to clients

Before version 0.9.0, settings used the FASTMCP_SERVER_ prefix (e.g., FASTMCP_SERVER_HOST). The old names FASTMCP_SERVER_HOST, FASTMCP_SERVER_PORT, and FASTMCP_SERVER_DEBUG still work but are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. item.title: Reson8 Open Sources Rumble-2-Flash: A 0.5B Speech Recognition Model
item.description:
Reson8 Open Sources Rumble-2-Flash: A 0.5B Speech Recognition Model

Reson8 has open-sourced Rumble-2-Flash, a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model, under the Apache 2.0 license. Designed for 40+ languages, the model competes with systems 3-60x its size while offering native support in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM without requiring custom code.

🧩 How it works

Rumble-2-Flash utilizes the Qwen3-ASR architecture to ensure day-0 support. To determine how small a model could become before accuracy degraded, the team distilled Rumble-2, a larger production model, into this smaller version using on-policy distillation.

In this process, the student model does not train on transcripts written by the teacher. Instead, it transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token. At every position, the teacher provides its own probability for the next token, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it receives corrections for the specific mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token rather than a single score per clip.

On-policy distillation typically requires the teacher and student to share a tokenizer, which was not the case here. Choosing Qwen3-ASR meant adopting its vocabulary, so the team introduced GOLD to remove this restriction. GOLD merges tokens where the two tokenizers split text differently, allowing both models to be compared over the same text. Tokens present in both vocabularies are compared directly, while others are compared via their sorted probabilities.

⚙️ Key details

  • Languages: Supports 40+ languages with automatic language detection.
  • Output Control: Allows numbers as digits or words, management of fillers, verbatim repeats, and forced language settings.
  • Performance: Processes an hour of audio in about half a second, achieving over 7,000 RTFx on full batches.
  • Benchmarking: On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track (Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch, and English), it averages a 6.96% error rate.
  • Comparison: This performance is better than Meta’s omniASR-LLM 7B (15x larger) and ahead of Whisper large-v3.
  • English Track: Averages a 6.6% WER.

On AppTek’s call-centre benchmark, which includes 302 hours of helpline calls and 14 English accents, Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER. This result is on par with NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78% and well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%). It is close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that performs better.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe 7.78% WER (On par with Rumble-2-Flash)

item.title: Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly
item.description:
Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly

Datasette Lite allows the full server-side Datasette Python web application to run directly inside a user’s browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide.

🧩 How it works

When the demo is launched, the browser downloads and executes a full Python interpreter, installs the datasette package and its dependencies, and starts the application in a Web Worker.

  • Datasette pages are displayed in a full-window <iframe> pointing to URLs under /app/<session>/.
  • A service worker (sw.js) intercepts requests (link clicks, form submissions, fetch calls, static assets) and relays them to the Datasette ASGI application running in Pyodide.
  • This architecture supports Datasette’s own JavaScript, plugin assets, POST forms, CSRF protection, sign-in cookies, and file uploads/downloads.
  • Streaming responses, such as server-sent events or CSV exports, are processed as they are produced.
  • If a client disconnects or aborts a fetch, the Datasette application is notified that the client has disconnected.
  • Cookies are stored in a cookie jar inside the Python ASGI bridge, lasting until the tab is closed or reloaded.

⚙️ Key details

  • Browser Requirements: Requires a browser with service worker support. Private browsing modes that disable service workers are not compatible.
  • Web Worker Support: Requires module workers (Chrome 80, Safari 15, Firefox 114 or later).
  • Python Version: Uses Python 3.14 from Pyodide 314.0.8.
  • Error Handling:
    • 503 returned if the tab has already been closed or reloaded.
    • 504 returned if the tab stops answering partway through a request (after four minutes).
    • 500 returned if the Pyodide worker itself fails.
    • 409 returned if a tab was opened before an incompatible update.
  • Session Management: Each tab receives a random session identifier, allowing multiple instances with different data to run simultaneously.
  • Navigation: The page mirrors the iframe’s location into its fragment to ensure the back button works and URLs are bookmarkable.
  • Security: Links to external sites open in a new window with noopener.

🚀 Availability and Versioning

Datasette Lite uses the most recent Datasette release from PyPI by default, including alpha and beta previews.

  • Stable Release: Append ?ref=stable to the URL.
  • Specific Release: Pass a version number as ?ref=.
  • Preview Release: ?ref=pre is equivalent to leaving ?ref out.
  • Source Code: Other ?ref values are treated as branches, tags, or commits in the simonw/datasette GitHub repository.
    • Example: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=main runs the latest development code.
    • Short SHAs made up only of digits are read as version numbers; full 40-character SHAs are required for specific commits.
    • ?ref values that look like version numbers are always installed from PyPI.
  • Plugin Installation: ?install= works for plugins, requiring a commit with a pyproject.toml.
  • CORS Handling: GitHub source zip files are downloaded through a Cloudflare Worker to add necessary CORS headers.

item.title: LLMKube Unifies LLM Inference Across GPU Fleets
item.description:
LLMKube Unifies LLM Inference Across GPU Fleets

LLMKube is a Kubernetes operator that manages LLM inference across heterogeneous GPU fleets, including NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple Silicon hosts. It turns deployment into a two-resource YAML setup and can expose models through an OpenAI-compatible API.

🔍 Overview

Define a Model and an InferenceService; the operator handles model downloading and caching, GPU scheduling, health checks, scaling, and API exposure. Linux GPU pods and Apple Silicon hosts both appear as InferenceService objects to kubectl.

🧩 How it works

The system has two cooperating processes:

  • An in-cluster controller manages Kubernetes-side desired state.
  • An optional out-of-cluster metal-agent is used for Apple Silicon hosts. It supervises OS-level processes and registers authenticated ingress with the cluster. An in-cluster relay fronts that ingress, so Metal InferenceService objects are ordinary Services.

On Apple Silicon, inference runs as native macOS processes rather than containers, allowing full Metal GPU access.

⚙️ Supported hardware and runtimes

Hardware or runtime Details in the evidence
NVIDIA CUDA support
AMD Vulkan support
Intel Listed among supported heterogeneous fleet hosts
Apple Silicon Metal support; native macOS inference processes
Runtimes llama.cpp, vLLM, TGI, and mlx-server
Apple Silicon processes The Metal Agent runs llama-server, mlx-server, and vllm-swift

Other capabilities include multi-GPU sharding, model caching, and running models across NVIDIA, Apple Silicon, and AMD from one spec.

🔐 Routing and policy

Adding a ModelRouter enables policy-aware routing between local models and external providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and LiteLLM. A rule matching requests labeled pii/phi by header can route only to local-tier backends. Content detection is planned (#441).

🚀 Availability and maturity

LLMKube is Apache-2.0 licensed, actively developed, and intended to run across homelab and on-prem fleets. It is pre-1.0: every CRD is v1alpha1, and fields can change between minor releases. For running one model on one laptop, Ollama is simpler.

SeaweedFS Offers Scalable O(1) Object and File Storage

SeaweedFS, a distributed storage system, has released a new iteration that enables scalable object storage and file serving.

🔍 Overview

SeaweedFS is a distributed storage system for object storage (S3), file systems, Iceberg table buckets, and Lance vector buckets, designed to handle billions of files with O(1) disk access and effortless horizontal scaling. SeaweedFS is a simple and highly scalable distributed file system. There are two objectives: 1. to store billions of files! 2. to serve the files fast!

🧩 How it Works

One SeaweedFS cluster serves an S3 object store, a POSIX file system, a lakehouse with S3 Tables and a built-in Iceberg REST Catalog, and vector search with S3 Vector Buckets, all on shared storage. Each blob is one disk read away, capacity grows by starting another volume server, and cloud storage can be cached or tiered transparently. Blob reads and writes have O(1) complexity and can run at the full speed supported by the underlying hardware.

NVIDIA Introduces Open Source SOMA Retargeter for Humanoid Motion Adaptation

The open source NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter adapts human motion data to fit a humanoid robot’s specific proportions, joint structures, and ranges of motion. Built around the shared human-motion representation in NVIDIA SOMA-X, the tool provides capabilities to configure robot embodiments, refine motion, and process trajectory data for downstream learning or control systems.

⚙️ How It Works

Directly copying human joint movement is not feasible for humanoid robots due to differences in physical structure. SOMA Retargeter adapts motion through a standardized workflow:

  • Input: Reads a Biovision Hierarchy (BVH) animation represented on the SOMA base skeleton.
  • Processing: Scales motion targets to the robot’s proportions, solves configured inverse-kinematics objectives for joint poses per frame, and applies configured post-processing corrections.
  • Output: Generates a comma-separated values (CSV) file containing the robot’s root position, orientation, and joint angles for each frame.

🧩 Compatible Motion Sources

Human motion inputs can be unified on the SOMA skeleton representation across multiple capture and generation methods:

Source / Tool Function Description
BONES-SEED Motion Capture Collection of human motion-capture data.
GEM-X Video Reconstruction Reconstructs whole-body 3D human motion from a single video using the SOMA body model.
Kimodo Motion Generation Generates human motion sequences from text and pose constraints on the SOMA skeleton.
ARDY Motion Generation Generates movement from text and pose constraints with interactive steering as motion unfolds.

🚀 SOMA Retargeter v0.2 Release

The v0.2 release includes sample motions from the BONES-SEED dataset, reference retargeting results, and pre-built configurations for five humanoid robot embodiments:

  • Unitree G1
  • Unitree H2
  • Booster T1
  • AgiBot X2 Ultra
  • AgiBot A3T3

To retarget a sample forward walk using the Unitree G1 configuration, users open a terminal in the repository root and start the viewer:

uv run python app/bvh_to_csv_converter.py --config assets/default_bvh_to_csv_converter_config.json --viewer gl

With unitree_g1 selected by default, selecting Retarget on the BVH Motion row under Scene Options → Motion executes the scaling, inverse-kinematics solving, and post-processing. The viewer displays the resulting robot animation alongside the source human motion.

🔍 Overview

When reviewing the Firefox network panel, requests to a Datasette table page were found to trigger an HTTP prefetch for the next page of rows in that table. This behavior was caused by Datasette pages serving an HTTP link header formatted as: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next"

⚙️ Key Details

  • Firefox has had an open issue regarding this HTTP prefetching behavior for 24 years.
  • An early comment on that 24-year-old issue links to a 2002 blog post written by the Datasette creator complaining about the feature.
  • The author had forgotten about both writing the blog post and the feature itself.

💡 Why It Matters

Automatic prefetching for next-page table rows creates unnecessary overhead:

  • Only a tiny fraction of visitors click the ’next’ link on a page.
  • The browser ends up fetching unnecessary data.
  • The Datasette server is forced to render an entire page that gets thrown away.

item.title: NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform adds open‑source tools for reliable GPU‑Kubernetes clusters
item.description:
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform adds open‑source tools for reliable GPU‑Kubernetes clusters

One underperforming GPU can slow an entire distributed training job, so measuring goodput – the volume of work successfully completed – is a more useful way to gauge cluster efficiency. NVIDIA’s DSX AI Factory Platform bundles the technologies needed to design, build, and operate efficient, resilient AI factories.

🔍 Overview

  • The platform’s open‑source software layer, NVIDIA DSX OS, provides tools for configuring, certifying, and maintaining the health of accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure.
  • It aims to keep every GPU, node, and network component in a ready state so that goodput remains high across large training jobs.

🛠️ Components

Component What it does
NVIDIA DSX OS Configures, certifies, and maintains accelerated Kubernetes clusters.
NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) Establishes a reproducible, version‑locked baseline for GPU‑optimized Kubernetes infrastructure; renders configuration recipes as bundles for existing deployment tools.
NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) Validates cluster readiness for production workloads; tests GPUs, networking, and storage with AI workloads and diagnostics; records certification results and flags faulty nodes.
NVSentinel Monitors cluster health; publishes node conditions based on GPU, node, and network health; cordons or taints unhealthy nodes, drains workloads, remediates faults, and can trigger re‑validation with NVCRE before returning nodes to service.

All three projects are licensed under Apache 2.0 and welcome external contributions.

⚙️ How it works

  • AICR defines the cluster’s software baseline in version‑controlled files and renders them into artifacts that any deployment tool can apply.
  • Declarative templates detect configuration drift from manual changes and keep node configurations consistent after repairs.
  • Each recipe entry pins a component version, declares required healthy dependencies, and includes a healthCheckAsserts block that runs after installation.
  • The health assertions filter on the container waiting reason rather than the pod phase alone.
  • The bundle command produces ready‑to‑use artifacts: 
    1

    aicr bundle --recipe recipe.yaml --deployer argocd --output ./bundles
  • The --deployer flag accepts helm, argocd, argocd‑helm, flux, or helmfile, so the same validated recipe can become Argo CD Application manifests, Flux resources, a Helmfile release graph, or plain Helm commands.
  • Because the recipe is a file, standard version‑control workflows (history, code review, drift detection) manage the baseline.
  • Drift detection can be enforced as a CI gate: 
    1

    aicr diff --baseline ./golden.yaml --target cm://default/aicr-snapshot --fail-on-drift

📊 Measuring Efficiency

  • Goodput focuses on the actual work completed, highlighting the impact of any slow GPU on overall training performance.

🚀 Availability

  • The DSX OS, AICR, NVCRE, and NVSentinel projects are all open source under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • External contributions are encouraged, and the tools integrate with common GitOps deployment pipelines.

item.title: Granite Timeseries Ensemble provides a zero‑training default forecast recipe
item.description:
Granite Timeseries Ensemble provides a zero‑training default forecast recipe

Granite Timeseries Ensemble (Granite TSFM) introduces a default, zero‑training forecast recipe that combines four pre‑trained models.

🔍 Overview

  • Pre‑trained time‑series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one.
  • Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default.
  • The default recipe combines four pre‑trained Granite models with different architectures, each capturing trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways.

🧩 How it works

  • Two main ensemble recipes are provided:
    • Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling)
    • IQR Ensemble (weights based on forecast spread)
  • Both recipes work with each member’s quantile forecasts (default 0.1 – 0.9) and produce a median and quantile forecasts.
  • Probabilistic Ensemble gives each member equal influence, pools quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles. No fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters are required.
  • IQR Ensemble approximates each member’s inter‑quartile range from the nearest 25th and 75th percentiles, then weights members inversely to their interval width. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step; isotonic regression keeps combined quantiles from crossing. A temperature setting and optional cap let users move weights toward uniform or limit any single member’s influence.

⚙️ Key details

  • Each member returns:
    • result.prediction_outputs – the point forecast.
    • result.quantile_outputs – quantile predictions ranging from 0.1 to 0.9.
  • The 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80 % coverage.
  • No retraining and no fitted ensemble weights; simple equal‑weight combinations have historically performed well in point forecasting.
  • The ensemble recipe stores the configuration rather than merged model weights; member checkpoints are downloaded at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run.
  • The recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed.
  • Both recipes were evaluated on 97 GIFT‑Eval dataset configurations (see the model card for full details, member checkpoints, evaluation, and limitations).

🚀 Availability

  • Install the package with: 
    1

    pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11"
  • Load the recommended four‑model recipe directly from Hugging Face.
  • The model card provides the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and known limitations.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a ready‑to‑use, zero‑training forecast solution for a wide range of series, from smooth industrial signals to noisy retail demand.
  • Reduces the risk of selecting a poor single model by combining diverse architectures; a 50‑year review of forecast combinations notes that such ensembles can lower error risk when members are high‑quality and diverse.
  • Enables applications to use the median as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast uncertainty without any hyperparameter tuning.

item.title: Open Responses API becomes vendor‑neutral standard with AWS Bedrock support
item.description:
Open Responses API becomes vendor‑neutral standard with AWS Bedrock support

The Open Responses open‑source specification has moved into a vendor‑neutral home under the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) and is now implemented at scale by Amazon Bedrock, giving developers a single API format for calling language models, streaming results, and orchestrating tool use.

🔍 Overview

  • The API format that a growing number of model providers use to call language models now has a vendor‑neutral home.\
  • Open Responses joined the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) as a project, bringing it under open governance alongside MCP and A2A.\
  • Open Responses is an open source specification that defines a single API format for calling language models, streaming results, and orchestrating tool use.\
  • AWS is involved in Open Responses and employs a core maintainer on the project; Amazon Bedrock already supports the Responses API across dozens of models.

🧩 How it works

  • Common request/response model – one schema for structured inputs and outputs that works across OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, local models, and any provider that implements the spec.\
  • Agentic loop – a unified pattern for models to emit tool calls, receive results, and continue reasoning, whether tools are developer‑hosted or provider‑hosted.\
  • Items as the atomic unit of context – a clear schema for messages, tool invocations, and reasoning state, with defined state machines (in_progress, completed, failed) for predictable behavior.\
  • Semantic streaming events – meaningful event types like response.output_text.delta and response.completed rather than raw text deltas, so clients can be built once and work across providers.\
  • Extensibility without fragmentation – provider‑specific tools and item types are namespaced with provider slugs, keeping the portable core clean while preserving room for innovation.

⚙️ Key details

  • OpenAI pioneered the Responses API for stateful conversations that call external tools or functions.\
  • Anthropic’s Messages API and Google’s Gemini API use different conventions; Open Responses standardizes these concepts with versioning, compliance tests, and extensibility rules.\
  • AWS is a member of the AAIF Governing Board and contributes to Open Responses’ development as an AAIF project.\
  • By housing Open Responses under AAIF alongside MCP and A2A, the specification evolves through community consensus, not any single company’s product roadmap.\
  • Bedrock’s implementation provides a production‑grade reference for how the spec works at scale.

🚀 Availability

  • Amazon Bedrock has supported the Responses API since December 2025 and continues to expand its implementation.\
  • Developers can use the familiar OpenAI SDK to call models hosted on Bedrock simply by changing the base URL and API key.\
  • Bedrock’s Responses API support includes:
    • Stateful conversation management via previous_response_id (no need to pass the full conversation history with each request).
    • Built‑in tool use for agentic workflows, including developer‑hosted and server‑side custom tools (server‑side tool support added in January 2026).
    • Streaming and non‑streaming modes across both bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints.
    • Broad model availability – the Responses API works with models from Amazon, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Google, and others, all through the same API format.
  • Existing applications built against the OpenAI Responses API can run on Bedrock with minimal changes, gaining access to Bedrock’s features such as Guardrails, cross‑Region inference, and intelligent prompt routing while keeping the same client code.
  • Recent additions include WebSocket transport for persistent connections and a compaction endpoint for managing long conversation contexts.

💡 Why it matters

  • For developers – one schema and compliance tests mean integration code can be written once and reused across providers.\
  • For model providers and inference platforms – Open Responses gives a clear specification to implement, avoiding the need to learn multiple proprietary APIs.\
  • Community governance – the AAIF framework ensures the spec evolves through consensus, fostering interoperability across the rapidly expanding landscape of language‑model providers.

#OpenResponses #AWS #AIAPIs #AgenticAI

Source: Open Responses Joins AAIF with AWS Support | Amazon Web Services

  • Total parameters: 501 billion (requires multi‑GPU deployment).
  • Active parameters: 23 billion (drive per‑token compute).
  • Effective context length: 1 million tokens.
  • The large parameter count shapes checkpoint storage, weight memory, sharding, and parallelism, while the active parameters affect per‑token compute.

item.title: llama.cpp v0.4.0 Released with 18 Backends and 1-Bit Quantization
item.description:
llama.cpp v0.4.0 Released with 18 Backends and 1-Bit Quantization

The llama.cpp project, a pure C/C++ LLM inference engine, has released stable version v0.4.0 on 2026-09-04, alongside a rapid cadence of 12 nightly builds in approximately 27.5 hours. The release extends the engine’s reach with 18 backend directories and introduces experimental 1-bit quantization, furthering its goal of “minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of hardware.”

🔍 Overview

llama.cpp is an inference engine built on the ggml library. Its README states the goal up front: LLM (and VLM) inference “with minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of hardware.” The latest stable release, v0.4.0 on 2026-09-04, is the only numbered release among the last 100; everything else is b108xx nightly builds pouring out with merges. Public since 2023-03-10, the cadence has held for over three years.

🧩 How it works

The engine uses a modular backend system. The ggml/src/ directory holds 18 matching backend directories. A registry in ggml/src/ scans, loads libraries, and picks the highest-scoring backend — each backend advertises its own capability in the same header, and the dispatcher trusts only that number.

For models larger than total VRAM, the README describes a hybrid mode: part runs on GPU, the rest falls back to CPU.

⚙️ Key details

Quantization support

The README lists the range — 1.5-bit, 2-bit, 3-bit, 4-bit, 5-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit integer quantization “for faster inference and reduced memory use.” Most striking is IQ1_S/IQ1_M — super-block 1-bit quantization: each weight keeps roughly one bit of information, and the model still generates tokens.

The enum in ggml.h spans 1-bit (IQ1_S/M), 4-bit (Q4_K, MXFP4) to 8-bit (Q8_0) — 56 type definitions in one header.

All compression kernels live in ggml-quants.c — 5,667 lines of C.

Supported backends

The “Supported backends” table in the README lists 17 backends — from CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, and HIP to Hexagon for Snapdragon, WebGPU for browsers, and even IBM zDNN.

Model format

The models doc says it plainly: “requires the model to be stored in the GGUF file format” — other formats must be converted with the Python scripts shipped in the repo. The key-value structure is so lean the API is declared in just 211 lines of gguf.h — a spec you can read in one sitting.

Contribution policy

The repo governs AI contributions with a “100% responsible for every line” policy and ships its own contribution-guidance skill in-tree. The first principle: “AI-generated code is allowed. What is not allowed is submitting code you do not understand.” Contributors own 100% of every line, whoever typed it — because every merged line is maintained indefinitely by a small maintainer team across a vast platform-backend matrix.

Measurement tools

Alongside sit the measurement tools: tools/quantize to compress, tools/imatrix to measure an importance matrix before compressing, tools/perplexity and tools/llama-bench to verify quality after — compress, then measure; never compress and trust.

🚀 Availability

Stable release v0.4.0 on 2026-09-04, yet 12 nightly b108xx builds landed in ~27 hours (per GitHub API on 2026-09-08). The repo’s pushed_at falls in the same window — 11:36:37 UTC on 2026-09-08.

💡 Why it matters

llama.cpp aims for performance across a “wide range of hardware” — x86, Apple Silicon, down to phone NPUs. With 18 backends and quantization as low as 1-bit, it enables running LLMs on devices that lack dedicated GPUs, while the hybrid GPU/CPU mode handles models larger than total VRAM. Inference configs for local LLMs are provided, including ready-to-run settings for Ollama Modelfile, vLLM command, and llama.cpp itself.

item.title: Dogwood Local Engine released as Apache‑2.0 library for temporal policy enforcement
item.description:
Dogwood Local Engine released as Apache‑2.0 library for temporal policy enforcement

Today we are releasing the Dogwood Local Engine under the Apache 2.0 license. The engine embeds the Dogwood governance language to enforce agent actions with temporal conditions.

🔍 Overview

  • Dogwood is an open source governance language for agents and their actions, released in August.
  • Policies specify which actions an agent may take and under what conditions, including temporal conditions that refer to past actions and outcomes.

🧩 How it works

  • The engine can be embedded as a library into an enforcement layer that regulates agents’ tool calls.
  • It maintains a durable record of past actions, tracking the order, timing, and outcomes so it can survive crashes and restart.
  • Only request events receive allow/deny verdicts; response events record outcomes (e.g., test pass/fail) used by temporal clauses.
  • An event is a timestamped record of one step of a tool call. A tool call typically generates a request event and a response event, forming the history evaluated by the engine.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supports dynamic policy updates without pausing workflows.
  • Example policies:
    • run_tests: the agent may always run the tests.
    • push_after_green_tests: the agent may push only when a test run has passed within the last fifteen minutes and no run has failed since. The when temporal clause expresses this condition.
  • The temporal clause is evaluated against the event history; it depends on events that happened before the request.

🚀 Availability

  • Released under the Apache 2.0 open source license.
  • Available as a local engine library that can be embedded.

💡 Why it matters

  • Allows policies to depend on past actions, their outcomes, order, and timing.
  • Guarantees enforcement after crashes because the engine stores history durably.
  • Supports policy changes during a session without stopping the workflow.

item.description:
AWS Labs releases TOLAP: Open‑source tool‑object level access control

TOLAP (Tool‑Object Level Access Protocol) is now available as an open‑source project under Apache‑2.0. It provides a specification and libraries that let teams enforce fine‑grained access policies at the data source.

🔍 Overview

  • “Tool‑Object Level Access Protocol (TOLAP) closes that gap.”
  • Role‑based access control answers whether a user can reach a resource, while attribute‑based access control evaluates policy at a centralized engine.
  • Database row‑level security is genuinely enforcement at the source — and it’s worth using.
  • Guardrails constrain what the model says, and agent frameworks such as Amazon Bedrock Agents, Azure AI Agent Service, Google Vertex AI Agents, and LangChain authorize whether the agent may invoke a tool.

🧩 How it works

  • Policy is applied where the data originates, not in a layer above it.
  • “The tool wraps the data source and enforces before anything crosses the boundary.”
  • Policies name individual data objects — columns, rows, fields, tags, endpoints, HTTP methods, similarity thresholds, storage prefixes, result limits.
  • The calling agent needs no security‑aware code.
  • “Your code fetches the data; TOLAP decides what may leave.”

⚙️ Key details

Component Description
Versioned policy schema Three layers: definition, assignment (links to user or group with scope and expiry), and merged effective policy that actually gets enforced. One schema spans databases, APIs, knowledge bases, and object storage.
Normative specification Defines canonical signing, the enforcement pipeline order, and the fail‑closed rules.
SDKs ( .NET, Python, TypeScript ) Each ships a core, store and enforcement package; core packages have zero external dependencies in all three languages.
Reference policy server & authoring console For teams who’d rather run a policy service than build one.
Integrations Fourteen tested integrations across the three languages, including MCP SDK, Strands, LangChain, LangChain.js, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, OpenAI Agents, Pydantic AI, Semantic Kernel, and Bedrock Agents.
  • TOLAP is not an MCP server and does not speak the MCP protocol.
  • It provides enforcement around the function your tool layer already calls.

🚀 Availability

  • “Today it’s available as open source under Apache-2.0 at github.com/awslabs/tolap.”
  • The repository contains the five items listed above and fourteen worked integrations with popular agent frameworks.

💡 Why it matters

  • Row‑level security and guardrails are essential for safe AI‑driven applications.
  • Agent frameworks need a way to authorize tool invocations; TOLAP supplies that capability.
  • By delivering a shared specification and ready‑made libraries, “every team doesn’t have to solve it from scratch,” accelerating secure AI development.

item.title: OWASP Recognizes Agent Memory Guard as an Official Incubator Project
item.description:
OWASP Recognizes Agent Memory Guard as an Official Incubator Project

The OWASP Foundation has officially recognized Agent Memory Guard as an Incubator Project, establishing it as an official project addressing memory and context poisoning (ASI06). Created and led by Vaishnavi Gudur with co-leader Anshul Rajkumar, the project provides a runtime defense designed to prevent AI agents from being weaponized through their own memory.

🔍 Overview

Modern AI agents persist memory across sessions, meaning anything written into that memory becomes a privileged input on the next turn. This introduces unique security vulnerabilities:

  • An attacker who plants text in the wrong field can override instructions, exfiltrate data, or hijack tool calls.
  • Because memory persists across sessions, the attack survives context resets.
  • While existing defenses run on user input at the front of the loop, memory poisoning runs directly on memory itself, presenting a completely different attack surface.

🧩 How it works

Agent Memory Guard addresses this vector by sitting directly between the agent and its memory store. It protects memory through the following mechanisms:

  • Operation Screening: It screens every operation through a pipeline of detectors and a declarative policy.
  • Tampering Detection: It uses SHA-256 baselines to flag out-of-band tampering with immutable keys.
  • Runtime Defense: It catches memory poisoning even after a context reset has occurred.

⚙️ Key details

The project offers a lightweight, local security implementation with the following specifications:

  • Minimal Integration: Requires only three lines of code to protect an agent’s memory.
  • No External Dependencies: Requires no API keys and makes no external calls.
  • Performance: Runs locally at a median latency of 59 µs.
  • Testing: Tested against 55 real-world attack payloads across 4 threat categories.
  • Industry Integration: Named in the Memory Hardening mitigation as an open-source implementation of memory-hardening controls. The architecture was discussed with practitioners in issue threads on microsoft/autogen, langchain-ai/langgraph, BerriAI/litellm, and 567-labs/instructor.

🚀 Availability

Developers can try the live Memory Poisoning Lab to run a representative attack-and-block scenario directly in a web browser.

Major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release.

📖 The Story Behind the Library

Every major library has a story. For huggingface_hub, it began with a simple idea: what if sharing machine learning models could be as easy as sharing code on GitHub?

In the early days of the Hugging Face Hub, researchers and practitioners faced a common frustration. Training a state-of-the-art model required significant compute resources and expertise. Once trained, these models often lived in isolation, stored on local machines and shared via (broken) Google Drive links. The AI community was duplicating work, wasting resources, and missing opportunities for collaboration.

The Hugging Face Hub emerged as the answer to this challenge. Initially, it was primarily used to share checkpoints compatible with the transformers library. All the Python code for interacting with the Hub lived within this library, making it inaccessible for other libraries to reuse.

In late 2020, we shipped huggingface_hub v0.0.1 with a simple mission: extract the internal logic from transformers and create a dedicated library that would unify how to access and share machine learning models and datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Initially, the library was as straightforward as a Git wrapper for downloading files and managing repositories. Five years and 35+ releases later, huggingface_hub has evolved far beyond its origins.

🏗️ The Foundation Years (2020-2021

The early releases established the basics. Version 0.0.8 introduced our first APIs, wrapping Git commands to interact with repositories. Version 0.0.17 brought token-based authentication, enabling secure access to private repositories and uploads. These were humble beginnings, but they laid the groundwork for everything that followed.

🔄 The Great Shift: Git to HTTP (2022)

In June 2022, version 0.8.1 marked a pivotal moment: we introduced the HTTP Commit API. Instead of requiring Git and Git LFS installations, users could now upload files directly through HTTP requests. The new create_commit() API simplified workflows dramatically, especially for large model files that are cumbersome to use with Git LFS. In addition, a git-aware cache file layout was introduced. All libraries (not only transformers, but third party ones as well) would now share the same cache, with explicit versioning and file deduplication.

This wasn’t just a technical improvement. It was a philosophical shift. We were no longer building a Git wrapper for transformers; we were building purpose-built infrastructure for machine learning artifacts that could power any library in the ML ecosystem.

📈 An Expanding API Surface (2022–2024)

As the Hub grew from a model repository into a full platform, huggingface_hub kept pace with an expanding API surface. Core repository primitives matured: listing trees, browsing refs and commits, reading files or syncing folders, managing tags, branches, and release cycles. Repository metadata and webhooks rounded up the offering so teams could react to changes in real time.

In parallel, Spaces emerged as a simple yet powerful way to host and share interactive ML demos directly on the Hub. Over time, huggingface_hub gained full programmatic control to deploy and manage Spaces (hardware requests, secrets, environment configuration, uploads). To deploy models on production-scale infrastructure, Inference Endpoints were integrated as well. Finally, the Jobs API came later (Q3 2025) to complete our compute offering.

The social and community layers became first-class citizens too: from APIs for pull requests and comments, to user and organization info, repository likes, following and followers, all the way through Collections to curate and share sets of related resources. Everyday ergonomics improved too: seamless authentication in Colab, resumable downloads, reliable uploads of large-scale folders, and more.

Then came version 0.28.0 and the Inference Providers ecosystem. Instead of a single inference backend, we partnered with multiple serverless providers (Together AI, SambaNova, Replicate, Cerebras, Groq, and more) to serve one API with transparent routing. We adopted a pay-per-request inference architecture that matched how people actually wanted to work.

⚡ Ready. Xet. Go! (2024-2025)

Version 0.30.0 introduced Xet, a groundbreaking new protocol for storing large objects in Git repositories. Unlike Git LFS, which deduplicates at the file level, Xet operates at the chunk level (64KB chunks). When you update a large file in a dataset or a model, only the changed chunks are uploaded or downloaded, not the entire file.

The migration was massive, starting with 20 petabytes across over 500,000 repositories. Yet it happened transparently, with full backward compatibility. One year later, all 77PB+ over 6,000,000 repositories have been migrated to the Xet backend, allowing for much faster (and smarter!) uploads and downloads. This happened with no user intervention, and no disruption to existing workflows 🔥

Progress chart showing the successful migration of 77PB+ across 6M+ repositories to the Xet backend

📊 Measuring Growth and Impact

Measuring the growth and impact of an open-source library is a tricky task. Numbers tell a story of their own:

  • 113.5 million monthly downloads, 1.6 billion total (October 2025)
  • Powers access to 2M+ public models, 500k+ public datasets, 1M+ public Spaces, and about twice as much when accounting for private repos
  • Used by 60k+ users daily, 550k+ monthly
  • Trusted by 200k+ companies from startups to Fortune 500

But the real scale becomes clear when you look at the ecosystem. huggingface_hub is a dependency for over 200,000 repositories on GitHub and 3,000 packages on PyPI, powering everything from major third-party frameworks like Keras, LangChain, PaddleOCR, ChatTTS, YOLO, Google Generative AI, Moshi, NVIDIA NeMo, and Open Sora, to countless smaller libraries and tools across the ML landscape. Our own ecosystem (transformers, diffusers, datasets, sentence-transformers, lighteval, gradio, peft, trl, smolagents, timm, lerobot, etc.) benefits from this foundation as well.

The remarkable part? Most of the third-party integrations happened organically, and we played no role in them. The Hugging Face Hub empowers the ML community in countless ways, yet we’re continually humbled by how far it has gone and how widely it’s used.

🏗️ Building for the Next Decad

Version 1.0 isn’t just about reaching a milestone. It’s about building the foundation for the next decade of open machine learning. The breaking changes we’ve made aren’t arbitrary; they’re strategic decisions that position huggingface_hub to scale with the explosive growth of AI while maintaining the reliability that millions of developers depend on.

🌐 Modern HTTP Infrastructure with httpx and hf_xet

The most significant architectural change in v1.0 is our migration from requests to httpx. This isn’t just dependency churn. It’s a fundamental upgrade that brings the library into the modern era of HTTP.

Why httpx? The benefits are substantial: native HTTP/2 support for better connection efficiency and true thread safety that enables safe connection reuse across multiple threads. Most importantly, httpx provides a unified API for both synchronous and asynchronous operations, eliminating the subtle behavioral differences that existed between our sync and async inference clients.

The migration was designed to be as transparent as possible. Most users won’t need to change anything. For those with custom HTTP backends, we’ve provided clear migration paths from configure_http_backend() to set_client_factory() and set_async_client_factory().

Additionally, hf_xet is now the default package for uploading and downloading files to and from the Hub, replacing the previously optional hf_transfer, which has now been fully removed.

🤖 Agents Made Simple with MCP and Tiny-Agents

Version 0.32.0 introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration and tiny-agents, fundamentally changing how developers build AI agents. What once required complex framework integration now takes approximately 70 lines of Python.

The MCPClient provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with tools, while the tiny-agents CLI lets you run agents directly from the Hub. Connect to local or remote MCP servers, use any Gradio Space as a tool, and build conversational agents that feel natural and responsive.

All of this is built on top of our existing InferenceClient and the dozens of Inference Providers it supports. We do believe Agents are the future, and huggingface_hub is there to provide the building blocks that enable AI builders to play with them.

💻 A Fully-Featured CLI for Modern Workflows

The CLI has evolved from a simple command-line tool into a comprehensive interface for ML operations. The streamlined hf command replaces the legacy huggingface-cli with a modern resource-action pattern:

  • hf auth login for authentication
  • hf download and hf upload for file transfers
  • hf repo for repository management
  • hf cache ls and hf cache rm for cache management
  • hf jobs run for cloud compute

The CLI comes with a sandboxed installer, making it easy to upgrade without breaking existing dev environments:

1
2
3
4
5

# On macOS or Linux
curl -LsSf https://hf.co/cli/install.sh | sh

# or on Windows
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://hf.co/cli/install.ps1 | iex"

With autocompletion support and an installer that works across platforms, the CLI now feels as polished as any modern developer tool.

🧹 Cleaning House for the Future

Version 1.0 removes legacy patterns that were holding us back. The Git-based Repository class is gone. HTTP-based methods like upload_file() and create_commit() are simpler, more reliable, and better suited for modern workflows. The HfFolder token management has been replaced with explicit login(), logout(), and get_token() functions. The old InferenceApi class has been superseded by the more feature-complete InferenceClient. hf_transfer has been fully replaced by hf_xet binary package.

These changes weren’t made lightly. Most deprecations were announced months in advance with clear warnings and migration guidance. The result is a cleaner, more maintainable codebase that can focus on forward-looking features rather than supporting deprecated patterns.

📋 The Migration Guide

We understand that breaking changes are disruptive. That’s why we’ve invested heavily in making the migration as smooth as possible. Our comprehensive migration guide provides step-by-step instructions for every change with explanations of why each change was necessary.

Most importantly, we’ve maintained backward compatibility wherever possible. HfHubHttpError, for example, inherits from both the old requests and new httpx base HTTPError classes, ensuring that error handling continues to work across versions. With this release, we’re fully committing to the future and we will focus exclusively on v1.0 and beyond, ensuring we can deliver the performance, features, and tools the community needs to interact with the Hugging Face Hub. Previous v0.* versions will remain available on PyPI, but they will only receive vulnerability updates.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release.

🙌 Credits

Originally posted at: https://huggingface.co/blog/huggingface-hub-v1

To our 280+ contributors who built this library through code, documentation, translations, and community support, thank you!

We’re also deeply grateful to the entire Hugging Face community for their feedback, bug reports, and suggestions that have shaped this library.

Finally, a huge thank you to our users - from individual developers to large enterprises - for trusting huggingface_hub to power your workflows. Your support drives us to keep improving and innovating.

Please star us on GitHub ⭐ to show your support and help us continue building the foundation of open machine learning. It has been five years, but it is still only the beginning!

🏁 Conclusion

The release of huggingface_hub v1.0 represents more than just a version number increment—it’s a testament to five years of community-driven innovation and the foundation for the next decade of open machine learning. With over 113.5 million monthly downloads, powering 200,000+ dependent libraries, and serving millions of users worldwide, this library has become the invisible infrastructure that makes AI accessible to everyone.

The strategic architectural changes in v1.0, from the migration to httpx and hf_xet to the introduction of MCP integration and the redesigned CLI, position the library to handle the explosive growth of AI while maintaining the reliability that millions of developers depend on. The careful balance between breaking changes and backward compatibility demonstrates a mature approach to software evolution—one that respects existing users while boldly embracing the future.

As we look ahead, huggingface_hub v1.0 isn’t just ready for the next wave of AI innovation—it’s built to enable it. From individual researchers sharing their first model to Fortune 500 companies deploying production AI systems, this library continues to democratize access to machine learning and foster the collaborative spirit that drives the field forward.
